🚀 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐂𝐓𝐄 – 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭-𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐇𝐢𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐞𝐬
========================================
Recently solved a fascinating SQL challenge that deepened my understanding of recursive CTEs and how they help in navigating hierarchical relationships like subsidiary chains.
Big thanks to Ankit Bansal for posting this insightful question really enjoyed working through it! 🙌

Problem Link : https://lnkd.in/euXKE-Kx
𝘎𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘯 𝘵𝘸𝘰 𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘴:
𝘚𝘶𝘣𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘪𝘢𝘳𝘺(𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘵, 𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘭𝘥)
𝘐𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘥(𝘤𝘯𝘢𝘮𝘦, 𝘱𝘯𝘢𝘮𝘦)
👉 𝘎𝘰𝘢𝘭: 𝘍𝘪𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘤𝘰-𝘪𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘳 𝘱𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘴 𝘣𝘺 𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘤𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘯𝘥𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘱𝘴 𝘢𝘤𝘳𝘰𝘴𝘴 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘵-𝘤𝘩𝘪𝘭𝘥 𝘴𝘶𝘣𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘪𝘢𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘴.

𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐫𝐲 (𝐔𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐄𝐋𝐅 𝐉𝐎𝐈𝐍) - (𝘓𝘪𝘮𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 1-𝘭𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘭 𝘏𝘪𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘳𝘤𝘩𝘺)
======================================

with cte_pc as(
select s1.parent as parent,s1.child as child, s2.parent as child_as_parent, s2.child as small_child from Subsidiary s1 
LEFT JOIN Subsidiary s2 ON s1.child = s2.parent)
, cte_level_1 as(
select * from Invested I LEFT JOIN cte_pc cp ON I.cname =cp.parent)
,cte_level_2 as(
select CONCAT(cl1.pname,',',cl2.pname) as pairs from cte_level_1 cl1 LEFT JOIN cte_level_1 cl2 ON cl1.small_child = cl2.cname where cl2.pname is NOT NULL)

select * from cte_level_2;

𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐫𝐲 (𝐔𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐂𝐓𝐄) :
=====================
-- Step 1: Build full parent-child hierarchy using recursive CTE
WITH PC_Hierarchy AS (
 SELECT parent, child FROM Subsidiary

 UNION ALL

 SELECT pc.parent, s.child
 FROM PC_Hierarchy pc
 INNER JOIN Subsidiary s ON pc.child = s.parent
)

-- Step 2: Find all co-investor pairs
SELECT CONCAT(I.pname, ',', I1.pname) AS co_investor_pairs
FROM Invested I
INNER JOIN PC_Hierarchy pc ON I.cname = pc.parent
INNER JOIN Invested I1 ON I1.cname = pc.child;

📸 Shared some images below clearly demonstrating:
-----------------------------------------------------------
✅ When a self join is sufficient (single-level hierarchy)
🔄 When you need a recursive CTE (multi-level hierarchy) and how recursive cte executes step - by -step

I'm excited to hear your thoughts and feedback at the end of this post. Let's continue learning and growing together!

#SQL #RecursiveCTE #DataAnalytics

ai_analysis.summary: The post presents a SQL challenge involving Subsidiary(parent, child) and Invested(cname, pname) tables. Its goal is to identify all co-investor pairs connected by direct or indirect parent-child relationships. It contrasts a self-join solution that is limited to a single hierarchy level with a recursive CTE that builds a multi-level parent-child hierarchy and then joins both endpoints to Invested to produce the pairs.
subtopics: Mapping hierarchy endpoints to investor names

interview_questions.question: How do the self-join and recursive CTE approaches differ in the hierarchy levels they traverse?
interview_questions.answer:
The self-join matches one Subsidiary child to another Subsidiary parent and is presented as sufficient for a single hierarchy level.
The recursive CTE repeatedly extends parent-child relationships and is used when indirect relationships span multiple levels.

interview_questions.question: Walk through how the recursive query turns the Subsidiary hierarchy into co-investor pairs.
interview_questions.answer:
The anchor member selects all parent-child rows from Subsidiary.
The recursive member matches PC_Hierarchy.child to Subsidiary.parent to extend the hierarchy while retaining the original root parent.
The query joins the root and resulting child to Invested on their cname values.
The two investor names are formatted with CONCAT to produce each co-investor pair.

interview_questions.question: A required relationship passes through more than one intermediate subsidiary. Why would the self-join solution be insufficient, and which query structure addresses it?
interview_questions.answer:
The self-join solution only extends Subsidiary once by matching a child to a parent, so it is limited to a single-level hierarchy.
The recursive CTE repeatedly applies the child-to-parent relationship, allowing the root parent to reach indirect descendants.
Both hierarchy endpoints can then be joined to Invested to identify the associated co-investor pair.

interview_questions.question: What roles do the Subsidiary and Invested tables play in the query?
interview_questions.answer:
Subsidiary supplies the parent and child relationships that define the hierarchy.
Invested maps a company name to an investor name that can be joined to hierarchy endpoints.
The final query uses Invested twice to obtain investor names for the parent and child sides of each relationship.
